Scientists just made quantum computer operations 1,000 times faster

📅 11 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1155 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Quantum computers remain highly vulnerable to errors and tiny disturbances from their surroundings.
  • According to recent reports, quantum computers could eventually transform areas such as drug discovery, energy technology, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and logistics.
  • A major challenge is that quantum computations can be disrupted by extremely small environmental effects.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Quantum computers remain highly vulnerable to errors and tiny disturbances from their surroundings. The longer a quantum operation takes to complete, the more time there is for those errors to build up. Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have now developed a method that can perform a broad range of advanced quantum operations more than a thousand times faster. The advance tackles a major obstacle in the field and could help move quantum computing closer to becoming fault-tolerant.

According to recent reports, quantum computers could eventually transform areas such as drug discovery, energy technology, cryptography, artificial intelligence, and logistics. Before that can happen, however, these machines need to become much more dependable.

Why Quantum Computers Are So Error-Prone.

A major challenge is that quantum computations can be disrupted by extremely small environmental effects. Electrical noise, cosmic radiation, and overheating can all introduce errors while information is being processed.

Recent findings suggest that traditional computers can experience errors too, but decades of development have produced reliable error correction methods that can rapidly detect and repair them. Quantum systems are much harder to protect because the information they use is extraordinarily delicate.

According to recent reports, "The fundamental building blocks of quantum computers, known as qubits, are so sensitive that even the smallest disturbance can cause the quantum state to deviate from the target, resulting in the loss of information. If too many errors accumulate before they can be corrected, the computation can fail," says Lei Du, researcher in Applied Quantum Physics at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden, and lead author of the theoretical study published in the journal Physical Review Letters.

A Different Way to Protect Quantum Information.

To make quantum computing more resilient and eventually fault-tolerant, researchers are investigating new ways to shield quantum information from errors. One promising strategy uses so-called bosonic quantum codes*.

Instead of assigning quantum information to individual qubits, this approach stores it in microwave fields inside superconducting circuits.

Sources indicate that "Rather than storing quantum information in individual qubits, bosonic codes encode information in the microwave fields found within superconducting circuits. This approach has been shown to provide stronger protection against certain types of errors," explains Tangyou Huang, researcher in Quantum Technology at Chalmers and co-author of the study.

Quantum Operations More Than 1,000 Times Faster.

Recent findings suggest that working with bosonic quantum codes is not simple. Creating and controlling the required quantum states has traditionally involved guiding a quantum system through thousands of repeated driving cycles.

That process can take considerable time, and every additional cycle creates another opportunity for outside disturbances to interfere with the calculation. In quantum computing, speed is therefore closely tied to reliability.

In a recent development, chalmers researchers Lei Du and Tangyou Huang have now proposed a different strategy. Rather than constructing the desired quantum states one small piece at a time, their method can perform a wide variety of operations much faster.

"Our method shows that a diverse range of quantum operations on bosonic states can be completed within a single driving cycle, rather than the several thousand cycles that have been required previously. This makes the operations both faster and more efficient, while reducing the risk that disturbances will corrupt the information before the process is finished. It represents an important step towards fault-tolerant quantum computers," notes Lei Du.

Quantum Lattice Gates Provide a Shortcut.

The new approach is built around Quantum lattice gates, a recently proposed universal set of quantum gates developed by the same research team.

It has been revealed that these gates act somewhat like shortcuts. Instead of requiring a long sequence of repeated control steps, they can allow the intended quantum operation to be completed in just one driving cycle. That could make the process faster, simpler, and less vulnerable to errors.

"You can think of it like building a large Lego castle. Instead of assembling it brick by brick and risking mistakes along the way, quantum lattice gates act like pre-built Lego modules that can be connected quickly and efficiently," says Tangyou Huang.

Designed for Superconducting Quantum Computers.

The technique is especially well suited to superconducting quantum computers, which are among the most prominent technologies being developed in the international push toward large-scale quantum computing.

Chalmers University of Technology is also using superconducting technology as it develops a 100-qubit quantum computer.

"A key advantage of our approach is that it can be implemented using existing superconducting quantum circuit platforms. We are already discussing possible experimental realizations with colleagues at Chalmers, and we hope to see a demonstration of the method in the near future," notes Tangyou Huang.

The researchers say the work addresses a central problem facing the field: efficiently producing and controlling quantum states that are capable of helping correct errors.

"Our results address one of the major bottlenecks in the field: how to quickly and reliably create and control the error-correcting quantum states that could play an key role in future quantum computers," says Lei Du.

More About Bosonic Codes, Quantum Lattice Gates and Floquet Control.

Sources indicate that *Bosonic quantum codes store quantum information in the states of, for example, microwave or optical resonators rather than in individual qubits. They are considered a promising tool for quantum error correction because they can provide built-in protection against certain types of errors.

Sources indicate that quantum operations are needed to process that stored information. Quantum lattice gates are a recently proposed collection of basic building blocks that can be used to control bosonic quantum states. By combining and designing these gates, researchers can carry out a wide range of more complicated quantum operations.

One method for implementing these operations is known as Floquet control, which uses periodic control signals to drive a quantum system. Earlier Floquet-based techniques have generally depended on slower processes involving many repeated driving cycles. The approach developed at Chalmers can instead perform quantum lattice gates directly in a single driving cycle, making some operations more than a thousand times faster.

Recent findings suggest that the scientific paper "Single-Period Floquet Control of Bosonic Codes with Quantum Lattice Gates" has been published in Physical Review Letters. The authors are Tangyou Huang, Lei Du, and Lingzhen Guo. The researchers are affiliated with Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden and Tianjin University in China.

The research was funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC), the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology (WACQT), and the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation.

Lenders back SpaceX's $43 billion Nvidia GPU deal but worry the collateral could end up in orbit, making them impossible to reclaim if Musk defaults

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elon Musk is borrowing $43 billion to finance SpaceX's acquisition of Nvidia AI chips for its ambitious data center projects and is using the semiconductors as collateral.
  • In a recent development, spaceX is working on building massive data centers on both Earth and in space.
  • Despite being one of the richest people on Earth right now, Musk is relying on a financing deal to acquire the chips he needs to achieve his dream of building an AI LLM that will “assist in the pursuit of understanding.” The $43 billion “Project Saturn” loan is also not structured like a typical loan, so its investment-grade rating would remain unaffected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk is borrowing $43 billion to finance SpaceX's acquisition of Nvidia AI chips for its ambitious data center projects and is using the semiconductors as collateral. However, Ars Technica reports that lenders are concerned that SpaceX will use the chips for its planned orbital data center, making it difficult, if not impossible, for creditors to reclaim in case the organization defaults on its loan. SpaceX stated it will deploy the collateralized chips only on Earth, but it remains unclear whether this provision is included in the signed debt instrument.

In a recent development, spaceX is working on building massive data centers on both Earth and in space. Musk has already revealed the firm’s first-generation AI1 satellite, with a 120-kilowatt payload and a span that’s larger than a Boeing 747, while he’s also planning to build a $24-billion gas-powered AI supercomputer in Starbase, Texas. These projects are in addition to the Colossus 1 and Colossus 2 sites near the Tennessee-Mississippi border.

Despite being one of the richest people on Earth right now, Musk is relying on a financing deal to acquire the chips he needs to achieve his dream of building an AI LLM that will “assist in the pursuit of understanding.” The $43 billion “Project Saturn” loan is also not structured like a typical loan, so its investment-grade rating would remain unaffected. Instead, it’s built similarly to aircraft leasing agreements, in which a leasing manufacturer buys the jets and leases them to the airline that wants to use them. This saves the airline from having to put up a significant amount of cash to get the airplanes that it needs.

For this deal, the Saturn Funding Trust, a fully owned subsidiary of asset-backed lending tech giant WHCO, would acquire the Nvidia GPUs for SpaceX, with the latter paying the former quarterly for the privilege of using the AI chips. The deal is also described as a “five-year triple-net, hell-or-high-water finance lease arrangement,” meaning SpaceX must pay the lease for five years, whether the chips break, become obsolete, or the project becomes unprofitable. It’s also responsible for all the expenses of operating the chips.

In a recent development, these terms are very lender-friendly, as SpaceX basically assumes all the risks while also keeping them off its books. Rating agency Moody’s also remarked in its report that the chips will be deployed in SpaceX’s U.S. data centers. Nevertheless, the manufacturer’s proposal to blast data centers into space is making some lenders nervous, regardless of its Earth-bound looks and promises.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Discord’s new Auto Clips automatically saves gameplay moments when it hears a voice chat erupt in laughter or shouting, and it’s rolling out to Nitro members now.
  • Whether you’re playing a chaotic game of Fortnite or getting your friends together for another big Minecraft marathon, being able to instantly capture those moments that leave you in stitches of laughter is imperative.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Discord’s new Auto Clips automatically saves gameplay moments when it hears a voice chat erupt in laughter or shouting, and it’s rolling out to Nitro members now.

Whether you’re playing a chaotic game of Fortnite or getting your friends together for another big Minecraft marathon, being able to instantly capture those moments that leave you in stitches of laughter is imperative.

After all, we’ve all been in situations where you’ve forgotten to hit record or your capture software has decided to stop working (it couldn’t be me). Enter Discord’s Auto Clips, a latest feature that can detect when your group starts laughing or shouting before pulling together a clip of what just happened.

According to recent reports, unlike other capture software, Discord Auto Clips removes the need to hit a keyboard shortcut to record clips. Instead, it uses a small machine learning model that runs locally on the user’s PC, which continuously looks for audio cues resembling laughter or shouting, then uses those reactions to flag moments that might be worth saving.

Discord has revealed that the model cannot understand conversations or identify individual speakers, while any footage that is not saved as a clip is discarded after the gaming session ends.

Auto Clips can also work without voice chat in Counter-Strike 2, Dota 2, League of Legends, and Rocket League. Discord uses integrations with those games to recognize events such as kills, goals, and completed rounds, with support for more titles planned in the future.

Recent findings suggest that we've been cooking on Clips since Early Access introduced in 2023.Now there's 🢂Ａｕｔｏ Ｃｌｉｐｓ🢀When you and your friends break out laughing in voice, Discord saves the moment. No keybinds or additional setup needed. Starting today, Auto Clips is rolling out to Nitro… pic.twitter.com/a70itXDB1f.

According to recent reports, up to three highlights can be saved during each session, after which players can review them through Discord’s Clips library. It’s here that each recording can be trimmed, renamed, and edited with text or images, while game and voice audio can be removed before you share it with your friends or the wider internet.

Discord testing latest “Game Mode” feature to help your PC run better.

Discord will soon let anyone find public server messages through Google.

Discord doubles Nitro upload limit to 1GB alongside server organization features.

Discord says clips remain stored locally on the player’s PC unless they choose to post them, and the company does not use saved footage, voice recordings, or other user data to train its detection model.

Sources indicate that if you want to opt out of the feature, Discord states that consumers will be able to disable Auto Clips entirely or prevent their voice from appearing in clips recorded by other people. The feature began rolling out to Nitro members in Early Access on November 24 and is right now only available through Discord’s Windows desktop app.

The model we're looking at here is the PlayStation 5 version, which is slightly cheaper than the PC model and comes with a few minor differences, such as using USB-C instead of USB-A and not having support for THX Audio. If you can stomach using the Razer Audio app instead of Synapse, and the lack of THX Audio support, which is, let's be honest, an edge case for general usage, then the BlackShark V2 Pro (PS5) is a great pickup, especially if you want to pick up a capable headset that works well across both PC and PS5 platforms. Tiny nanolaser could cut computer energy use in half

📅 11 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (639 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The development of a nanolaser could mark an early step toward a future in which microchips communicate entirely with particles of light.
  • Sources indicate that researchers at DTU have created a tiny nanolaser that could eventually help make computers, smartphones, and data centers faster while using much less energy.
  • In the future, thousands of these lasers could potentially be integrated onto a single microchip.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The development of a nanolaser could mark an early step toward a future in which microchips communicate entirely with particles of light.

Sources indicate that researchers at DTU have created a tiny nanolaser that could eventually help make computers, smartphones, and data centers faster while using much less energy. The breakthrough was published in the scientific journalScience Advances.

In the future, thousands of these lasers could potentially be integrated onto a single microchip. Instead of moving information around a chip with electrical signals, devices could transmit data using photons, the particles that make up light.

"The nanolaser opens up the possibility of creating a newly introduced generation of components that combine high performance with minimal size. This could be in information technology, for example, where ultra-small and energy-efficient lasers can reduce energy consumption in computers, or in the development of sensors for the healthcare sector, where the nanolaser's extreme light concentration can deliver high-resolution images and ultrasensitive biosensors," notes DTU professor Jesper Mørk.

It has been revealed that mørk co-authored the study with, among others, Drs. Meng Xiong and Yi Yu from DTU Electro.

Using Light Inside Computer Chips.

Much of the internet already relies on light to carry information through fiber optic cables. Inside computers, however, data still moves through electronic circuits using electricity. That approach produces heat and can limit how rapidly information can be transferred.

Recent findings suggest that nanolasers could bring optical communication directly onto microchips. By generating light signals efficiently inside the chip, they could allow information to move with very little energy loss, potentially making future devices faster, cooler, and more energy efficient.

Mørk estimates that using nanolasers in computers could reduce energy consumption by as much as half.

Sources indicate that the compact DTU nanolaser is an crucial step toward that goal. Future chips designed around light-based communication would likely require thousands of extremely small, efficient lasers working together to transmit information across the chip.

Breaking the Size Limit for Lasers.

Sources indicate that the upcoming nanolaser was created in DTU's clean room facility, DTU Nanolab. According to Mørk, the device pushes beyond the conventional limit for how small a laser can be made.

At its core is a structure known as a nanocavity, which traps and concentrates light within an exceptionally tiny space. Until now, achieving such intense confinement at this scale had been considered extremely difficult.

Industry observers note that when researchers shine a beam of light onto the device, both photons and electrons become concentrated in the same microscopic region. This interaction allows the laser to function at room temperature while requiring unusually little energy.

The light-trapping structure used in the nanolaser was originally developed by Professor Ole Sigmund's group at DTU Construct.

Faster Devices and Lower Energy Use.

Industry observers note that the next major challenge is making the nanolaser operate using electrical power. If researchers can achieve that, the technology could have broad applications across computing, communications, and healthcare.

Computers and smartphones could potentially deliver greater performance while consuming less electricity. Data centers, which require enormous amounts of power, could also see substantial reductions in energy use, potentially leading to significant climate benefits.

In healthcare technology, the nanolaser's ability to concentrate light into an extremely small area could support ultra-sensitive sensors and high-resolution imaging systems.

Researchers estimate that the remaining technical challenges could be solved within the next 5-10 years.

An influencer using AI prompts to score cheap upgrades on flights has reportedly ended up overpaying compared to normal prices.

Industry observers note that as artificial intelligence has become an everyday part of life for a lot of people, it has also helped travellers looking to plot out journeys. Many have used ChatGPT to scout out restaurant, hotels, and even score deals on flights. Though, others have fallen foul of fake AI ads for travel hotspots that don’t actually exist.

However, as per travel experts at One Mile at a Time, an influencer who has been advertising a ChatGPT script to get cheaper upgrades on flights, seemingly ended up overpaying.

MavGPT laid out three prompts for ChatGPT, including urging the AI to ask about what airmiles you have, as well as checking if a flight you’re booked on has any upgrade available. In his example, he claimed he was flying with American Airlines Los Angeles to London Heathrow, with the AI spending 52,000 miles and a $190 fee for the upgrade.

According to One Mile at a Time, MavGPT “got screwed” if that was the AI’s best idea, seeing as it took the instant upgrade offer that the airline offer anyway.

They added that it wasn’t an “actual trick or hack,” and the AI should have looked at the “systemwide upgrade” seeing as there were still empty seats available.

“While there are definitely some strong use cases for AI, I think this is actually a pretty poor showing of what it can do,” they added, noting that the miles could have easily been saved and spent on “something else” instead.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, moore Threads’ MTT S80 product manager notes that the next Lushan gaming GPU will have more VRAM than any consumer graphics card currently available, VideoCardz reports.
  • Moore Threads apparently hasn’t given up on graphics, even four years after the MTT S80’s release.
  • Although nothing the product manager stated is an official statement, his words suggest that the upcoming Lushan GPU could feature the largest memory capacity yet offered on a consumer graphics card, which certainly draws a lot of attention from gamers and local AI enthusiasts alike.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, moore Threads’ MTT S80 product manager notes that the next Lushan gaming GPU will have more VRAM than any consumer graphics card currently available, VideoCardz reports. With Nvidia’s RTX 5090 already at 32GB, Lushan would need more than that. This matches the previous promise of four times the company’s MTT S80’s 16GB, putting the flagship Lushan at 64GB.

Moore Threads apparently hasn’t given up on graphics, even four years after the MTT S80’s release. The tech giant teased the card earlier this week with a poster for MDC 2026, its developer conference, showing a graphics card under a black cloth on a mountainside, and put Lushan’s name in the title of the post. It has previously indicated that Lushan products would arrive before the end of the year.

Although nothing the product manager stated is an official statement, his words suggest that the upcoming Lushan GPU could feature the largest memory capacity yet offered on a consumer graphics card, which certainly draws a lot of attention from gamers and local AI enthusiasts alike. As it stands, the 32GB RTX 5090 was available at $6,599 in our recent Newegg check, more than three times its MSRP, which illustrates the astronomical demand.

Not disclosed; “4x” the S80 claimed, up to 64GB by our math.

Recent findings suggest that $1,999 MSRP; from $6,599 at Newegg (Nov. 15).

According to recent reports, 2,999 yuan with a motherboard (about $410) at launch; 1,499 yuan (about $225) at JD.com, Nov. 21.

Intel Arc Pro B60 Dual (Maxsun).

The Lushan would be a graphics rendering chip based on the Huagang architecture, with a sibling Huashan for AI. Performance claims are lofty at 15x for AAA gaming, 50x ray tracing, 64x AI compute, and 16x geometry processing over the MTT S80, based on information from MDC 2025, last year’s edition of the conference. To get there, Lushan adds a latest hardware ray-tracing engine, the UniTE rendering architecture, AI generative rendering, which MyDrivers describes as the manufacturer’s answer to Nvidia’s DLSS and AMD’s FSR for upscaling and multi-frame generation, and DirectX 12 Ultimate support.This is a mighty high goal, as the previous outing, with the S80, fell short of expectations. Released in November 2022 at 2,999 yuan (about $410), the S80 was at first sold only in a bundle with an Asus motherboard. It now costs about half that in China, despite rising GPU costs. The 16GB GDDR6, PCIe 5.0 GPU, which pulls 255W, only matched a low-end card when tested on immature drivers in early 2023; it struggled against a GT 1030.

Moore Threads stated last December that it had shipped monthly driver updates since and claimed the S80 then benchmarked 3.4x higher than at launch. The new 15x target is more reasonable when put against the backdrop of just how far the S80 trailed when it landed.

Industry observers note that if we look beyond the consumer space, there are plenty of cards that have more than 32GB, and 64GB for that matter. The Nvidia RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell workstation card, for instance, has 96GB of GDDR7. It’s also possible to get RTX 4090s rebuilt with 48GB, at least in some Chinese shops, and a listing in September offered an RTX 5090 modded to 96GB. Maxsun also has the Arc Pro B60 Dual, built on Intel GPUs, with 2x 24GB on just one board. However, memory supply remains tight, with crushing memory shortages, and is projected to remain so, while GDDR7 remains quite costly.

In a recent development, domestic rival Lisuan’s G100, meanwhile, is only at 12GB and 24GB for consumer and enterprise. A 64GB Lushan would leave those in the dust, which may hint that Moore Threads is targeting Western cards rather than just domestic rivals. It also raises the question of just how much memory you need for certain workloads.

#172367. AI uncovers hidden Ozempic side effects across 400,000 Reddit posts

📅 13 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1562 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

AI uncovers hidden Ozempic side effects across 400,000 Reddit posts

📅 13 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1562 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artificial intelligence is giving researchers a upcoming way to listen to what patients are saying about popular GLP-1 drugs.
  • Industry observers note that the study, published recently in Nature Health, examined more than five years of posts from nearly 70,000 Reddit users.
  • The findings do not establish that the medications caused these symptoms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artificial intelligence is giving researchers a upcoming way to listen to what patients are saying about popular GLP-1 drugs. After analyzing more than 400,000 Reddit posts, a University of Pennsylvania team identified several symptoms reported by people using semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy, and Rybelsus) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro and Zepbound) that may not be fully represented in clinical trials or official regulatory information.

Industry observers note that the study, published recently in Nature Health, examined more than five years of posts from nearly 70,000 Reddit users. Two categories stood out as particularly deserving of further investigation: reproductive symptoms, including changes in menstrual cycles, and problems involving body temperature, such as chills and hot flashes.

The findings do not establish that the medications caused these symptoms. Instead, researchers say the massive collection of spontaneous patient reports may reveal signals worth examining more closely.

"Some of the side effects we found, like nausea, are well known, and that demonstrates that the method is picking up a real signal," says Sharath Chandra Guntuku, Research Associate Professor in Computer and Information Science (CIS) at Penn Engineering and the study's senior author. "The underreported symptoms are leads that came from patients themselves, unprompted, and clinicians could potentially pay attention to them.".

What Patients Report Outside Clinical Trials.

Clinical trials are designed to determine whether treatments work and to identify important safety problems, but they cannot necessarily capture every symptom that matters to patients once a medication is being used by a much larger population.

"Clinical trials generally identify the most dangerous side effects of drugs," adds Lyle Ungar, Professor in CIS and a co-author on the study. "But they can fail to find what symptoms patients are most concerned about; even though social media is not necessarily representative, a large collection of posts may reflect additional concerns.".

Industry observers note that the distinction is notable. The study found associations in what people discussed online, not proof that GLP-1 drugs were responsible for those experiences.

In a recent development, "We can't say that GLP-1s are actually causing these symptoms," notes Neil Sehgal, the study's first author and a doctoral student in CIS advised by Guntuku and Ungar. "But nearly 4% of the Reddit users in our sample reported menstrual irregularities, which would be even higher in a female-only sample. We think that's a signal worth investigating.".

Using Social Media as an Early Health Signal.

The idea of mining online conversations for clues about drug safety predates today's AI boom. In 2011, Ungar participated in one of the earliest efforts to use material created by internet customers to identify possible adverse effects from medications.

Social media can capture experiences that patients discuss with one another but may never formally report to a doctor, drug manufacturer, or regulator.

Recent findings suggest that "Online patient communities work a lot like a neighborhood grapevine," says Ungar. "People who are living with these medications are swapping notes with each other in real time, sharing experiences that rarely make it into a doctor's office visit or an official report.".

According to recent reports, since then, online patient communities have expanded enormously. That has made social media a potentially valuable source for studying how medications affect people in everyday life, although gaining access to platform data has become more difficult.

Traditional clinical research remains essential, the researchers emphasize, but online conversations can provide information far more rapidly when millions of people begin using a drug.

Recent findings suggest that "Clinical trials are the gold standard, but by design, they are slow," says Guntuku. "This is not a replacement for trials, but it can move much faster, and that speed matters when a drug goes from niche to mainstream almost overnight.".

AI Makes Massive Social Media Analysis Possible.

One of the biggest obstacles has always been scale.

Guntuku describes the approach as "computational social listening," which uses computational methods to identify patterns in large collections of online conversations about health.

According to recent reports, patients, however, rarely describe symptoms using standardized medical terminology. One person might describe feeling unusually cold, another might mention constant chills, while a clinician could categorize those experiences using a specific medical term.

In a recent development, researchers therefore need a way to translate everyday language into standardized categories. One important reference is the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA), which provides terminology widely used to classify medical conditions, symptoms, and adverse events.

Previously, connecting huge numbers of informal social media posts with standardized medical terminology required enormous amounts of work, limiting how much data researchers could realistically analyze.

Large language models such as GPT and Gemini are changing that equation by allowing researchers to process and categorize vast amounts of text more consistently and swiftly.

"Large language models have made it possible to do this kind of analysis much faster with a level of standardization that could be difficult to achieve before," states Sehgal.

Unexpected Symptoms Emerge From 400,000 Posts.

The researchers stress that Reddit users do not represent the overall population of people taking GLP-1 drugs. Reddit users tend to be younger, are more likely to be male, and are disproportionately located in the United States.

According to recent reports, even with that limitation, the analysis produced a reassuring sign that the approach was detecting genuine patterns. Many of the symptoms discussed by Reddit users closely matched already known effects of semaglutide and tirzepatide.

It has been revealed that about 44% of people included in the study described at least one side effect. Gastrointestinal problems were the most common, consistent with the nausea and other digestive challenges already associated with these medications.

More intriguing were symptoms that appeared frequently enough to attract the researchers' attention but may not be as well represented in current drug labels or conventional adverse event reports.

It has been revealed that nearly 4% of people who reported side effects described reproductive symptoms. These included changes in menstruation such as bleeding between periods, heavy bleeding, and irregular menstrual cycles.

People also described changes involving body temperature, including chills, feeling unusually cold, hot flashes, and symptoms resembling a fever.

According to recent reports, fatigue was another notable finding. It was the second most frequently reported complaint in the Reddit data, even though relatively few clinical trials reported fatigue often enough for it to reach established reporting thresholds.

Why Menstrual and Temperature Changes Are Interesting.

Sources indicate that one possible reason these reports caught researchers' attention involves the hypothalamus, a small but extremely notable region of the brain. Among its many jobs, the hypothalamus helps regulate hunger, hormones, reproduction and body temperature.

Sources indicate that "These drugs are thought to work by engaging part of the brain called the hypothalamus, which helps regulate a wide variety of hormones," notes Jena Shaw Tronieri, Senior Research Investigator at Penn's Center for Weight and Eating Disorders and a co-author of the study. "That doesn't mean the medications are necessarily causing these symptoms, but it could suggest that reports of menstrual changes and body temperature fluctuations are worth studying more systematically.".

Recent findings suggest that the researchers are not proposing that this biological connection proves GLP-1 drugs are responsible. Instead, it offers another reason to test the patient-reported patterns more carefully through controlled research.

Turning Online Conversations Into Research Leads.

For now, the team hopes the results encourage scientists and clinicians to pay closer attention to symptoms that patients repeatedly discuss online.

"They're clearly on patients' minds, and that's worth paying attention to," states Sehgal.

Sources indicate that the researchers also want to broaden their analysis beyond Reddit and beyond English-language communities. Doing so could help determine whether the same patterns emerge among different groups of people and on different social media platforms.

"We don't really know yet whether what we're seeing on Reddit reflects the experience of GLP-1 owners globally, or whether it's particular to the kind of person who posts on Reddit in the United States," Ungar notes.

In the longer term, rapid AI analysis of online patient conversations could potentially become an early detection system for emerging health concerns involving drugs, supplements and wellness products.

Sources indicate that that could be particularly valuable for substances that become popular online faster than conventional research can keep up. Loosely regulated or unregulated products, including injectable peptides, can spread quickly through communities on Reddit, TikTok and other platforms. Discussions among owners may therefore provide some of the earliest indications of unexpected effects.

"The whole point of this kind of approach is that it can move quickly, and that's exactly when it's most valuable," notes Guntuku.

According to recent reports, this study was conducted at the University of Pennsylvania School of Engineering and Applied Science. The authors report no outside funding. Tronieri reports receiving an investigator-initiated grant, on behalf of the University of Pennsylvania, from Novo Nordisk and receiving consulting fees from Currax Pharmaceuticals, LLC. The other authors report no conflicts of interest.

#172366. AI agents design an entirely latest CPU architecture from scratch, startup claims

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1106 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

AI agents design an entirely latest CPU architecture from scratch, startup claims

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1106 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Architect Labs, a Palo Alto startup, mentioned in a research blog post that its AI systems discovered, designed, and verified Frostbite, a general-purpose CPU with a newly introduced instruction set “built from the ground up.” Across 25 workloads, a four-tile Frostbite cluster delivered 4.59 times the performance per watt of a similarly sized “silicon-proven” dual-matter, in-order CPU core.
  • Conventional CPUs have hardware that “rediscovers, at runtime, which instructions actually depend on each other.” Multicore designs also need deep cache hierarchies and coherence protocols, which keep every core’s view of shared memory consistent, but scale poorly and cost area and power.
  • Frostbite’s programs are compiled to interaction nets, a model of computation from 1990 in which a program is a graph of nodes and computation happens by rewriting pairs of connected nodes, and the chip is designed around this distinct paradigm.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Architect Labs, a Palo Alto startup, mentioned in a research blog post that its AI systems discovered, designed, and verified Frostbite, a general-purpose CPU with a newly introduced instruction set “built from the ground up.” Across 25 workloads, a four-tile Frostbite cluster delivered 4.59 times the performance per watt of a similarly sized “silicon-proven” dual-matter, in-order CPU core. Those numbers come from a simulated 7nm design that has not yet been made in silicon, and the company claims it can’t name the comparison core for legal reasons.

Conventional CPUs have hardware that “rediscovers, at runtime, which instructions actually depend on each other.” Multicore designs also need deep cache hierarchies and coherence protocols, which keep every core’s view of shared memory consistent, but scale poorly and cost area and power. Architect Labs’ alternative is what it calls “multithreading for free,” where the program itself exposes the parallel work, without threads, locks, or out-of-order hardware required for that discovery.

Frostbite’s programs are compiled to interaction nets, a model of computation from 1990 in which a program is a graph of nodes and computation happens by rewriting pairs of connected nodes, and the chip is designed around this distinct paradigm. Pairs of nodes being rewritten never overlap, so they can run in any order, or all at once, and arrive at the same result. Every value is also used exactly once, so data can stay in small local memories instead of large shared caches.

An example of the difference given by the team is a 5x5 chess-like board with five queens, placed so none can attack another. A typical program searches for solutions one board at a time. As an interaction net, the same search breaks into 3,183 small operations, and the longest chain that has to run in order is only 262 steps, so on average about 12 operations are ready to run at once at each step. Nothing about the program was rewritten to get there, as the parallel work was already intrinsic.

Sources indicate that each of the chip’s tiles, small identical processing units linked by an on-chip network, has its own small local memory. Four tiles, plus four L3 nodes, form the cluster that’s benchmarked against the conventional core for the performance claims, but the full layout has 16 tiles. The design reached 800 MHz in early synthesis but ended up at 500 MHz in the final layout. The cluster also averaged 8.77 times the comparison core’s performance per area, and the table below indicates how its performance per watt varies by workload.

Industry observers note that frostbite performance per watt vs. comparison core.

15 held out until the final evaluation.

Worst: recursive Fibonacci (held out).

According to recent reports, it may come as some surprise that the AI which built Frostbite started with what the manufacturer calls “zero architectural priors,” though the team first picked the workloads it had to do well on, and this sort of blank slatism may have its advantages in avoiding bias. Instead, the agents read papers and benchmarks, built Python models, and then selected one concept for focus. The original 141-page PDF output, which contained a programming model, runtime, and high-level blocks, was deleted after the first register-transfer level (RTL) design was generated, because “many of the numbers and estimates were well off what was physically possible.”.

That PDF was only ever a starting point. Once the agents picked an architecture, they moved away from English — as it can’t get every detail right or catch every mistake, according to the team — and wrote the spec in the manufacturer’s own language, called ASL. ASL translates to Lean, a proof checker, so it can be machine-checked, which the company indicates stops a large class of bugs and cuts down on agents gaming their objectives. From this, the agents devised Arcmodel, a software model of the whole chip written in ASL, before any circuit design existed.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Recent findings suggest that simulating the RTL is slow, so the agents tested ideas on the model instead, which ran about 200 times faster. At first, the model’s power estimates were off by up to almost 250%, but an automated loop adjusted it until it matched the circuit design within just 5%.

It has been revealed that from there, swarms of agents proposed changes in parallel, and each one was checked against the spec, tried in the fast model, built into the circuit design, and measured for power before being kept or dropped. This led to 58 ideas tried, with 37 kept. Separately, a behavior emerged that “was never specified by any human,” in what is known as work stealing: a tile with nothing to do can pull spare work from a neighbor or, in lieu of anything to do, go idle to save power.

Share of energy (one four-tile cluster, mean of 20 workloads, excluding clock distribution).

Fetching, decoding, and issuing instructions.

Clock distribution (share of total energy, left out of the rows above).

This isn’t Architect Labs’ first design, as it showed off Redwood, an AI inference accelerator for robots and drones, in August. In that case, the organization says its AI generated the RTL, verification, firmware, drivers, and kernels in under two weeks from a spec written by two human architects. Redwood still runs only on an FPGA and hasn’t been made in silicon, though the company says it is working toward having it built at TSMC.

Tendrils Compute, a possible rival based in Cambridge, U.K., raised funding earlier this month for a processor it indicates will have “thousands of cores operating in parallel.” It is also developing Vine, the same language Frostbite’s programs are written in.

Architect Labs says more benchmarks are coming, but they’re only part of the blueprint. It also wants an FPGA-hosted “software playground for anybody to run a program on Frostbite” along with a “preliminary operating system.” Eventually, it intends to release Frostbite’s RTL and instruction set.

Sources indicate that in the meantime, the company plans to cover more workloads and compare “a broader set of CPUs,” including larger Frostbite mesh configurations against multicore versions of the comparison core with large caches. It also plans to test against “larger, wider, out-of-order CPUs,” with these comparisons due in the coming months on popular CPU benchmark suites such as SPEC and PARSEC.

The shape behind the Einstein problem just revealed strange newly introduced physics

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A mathematical shape that drew global attention for solving a decades-old puzzle is now revealing an unexpected connection to physics.
  • In a study published in Nature Communications, researchers from the Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo, and collaborating institutions built optical structures inspired by the "Smith hat." This unusual shape is known for solving the so-called Einstein problem in mathematics.
  • The Einstein problem asks whether a single tile shape, known as a "monotile," can cover an entire surface without creating a repeating pattern.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A mathematical shape that drew global attention for solving a decades-old puzzle is now revealing an unexpected connection to physics. Researchers have found that structures based on the shape can make light form unusual chiral patterns, pointing to newly introduced ways of exploring how geometry can influence optical behavior.

In a study published in Nature Communications, researchers from the Institute of Industrial Science, The University of Tokyo, and collaborating institutions built optical structures inspired by the "Smith hat." This unusual shape is known for solving the so-called Einstein problem in mathematics. When the team illuminated the structures with laser light, they observed diffraction effects unlike those seen in conventional quasicrystals.

The Shape That Solved the Einstein Problem.

The Einstein problem asks whether a single tile shape, known as a "monotile," can cover an entire surface without creating a repeating pattern.

Recent findings suggest that familiar tilings such as checkerboards and honeycombs repeat in a regular way. An aperiodic monotile, by contrast, can fill a surface without ever settling into a repeating arrangement.

In a recent development, in 2023, researchers discovered the first such monotile, the Smith hat. The finding attracted widespread attention because it provided a long-sought solution to the mathematical problem.

It has been revealed that "What is especially fascinating about the hat tile is that, although the resulting pattern appears irregular at first glance, it is actually constructed from the honeycomb lattice," says lead author Yuto Moritake. "We wanted to see whether this unique shape could also produce any unexpected physical phenomena.".

Turning a Mathematical Pattern Into an Optical Structure.

To test that possibility, the researchers created nanoscale versions of the pattern on silicon nitride films using electron beam lithography.

Recent findings suggest that when laser light was directed at the structures, the resulting diffraction patterns formed distinctive pinwheel-like shapes. These patterns directly revealed the chiral character of the aperiodic structure.

Industry observers note that chirality refers to a form of handedness in which a structure and its mirror image cannot be perfectly matched. In this case, the unusual arrangement of the monotile pattern caused the light itself to display a chiral response.

According to recent reports, "We found that the diffraction patterns themselves become chiral because the structure lacks mirror symmetry," explains senior author Masaya Notomi. "This kind of optical response is fundamentally different from that observed in conventional quasicrystalline materials.".

Light Responds to Direction and Polarization.

The researchers also found that the diffraction pattern changed depending on both the direction and polarization of the incoming light.

When the physical structures were mirrored, their optical behavior reversed as well. This revealed that the response of the light was directly tied to the symmetry of the underlying pattern, revealing a fresh type of symmetry-controlled optical behavior.

It has been revealed that "These results open a new direction of research on the fusion of quasiperiodic order and chirality," remarks Moritake. "Monotile patterns provide a platform for exploring optical phenomena that emerge from the interplay of symmetry, chirality, and aperiodicity.".

From Abstract Mathematics to Latest Optical Physics.

The researchers say structures inspired by monotiles could eventually contribute to technologies designed to manipulate light, control polarization, and support advanced optical devices.

More broadly, the findings show how a discovery that began as an abstract mathematical puzzle can lead to unexpected physical effects. The Smith hat was first celebrated for solving a question about how shapes can cover a surface. Now, its unusual geometry may also help researchers uncover latest ways to control and study light.

Why you should upgrade to an OLED for GTA 6

💡 Key Takeaways
  • With GTA 6 bringing players back to Vice City, many are already thinking about how to get the most out of Rockstar’s next open-world game when it rolls out.
  • With neon-lit streets, crowded nightlife, tropical beaches and surrounding landscapes of Leonida, GTA 6 is Rockstar’s most visually ambitious release yet.
  • While much of the conversation is focused on how consoles will handle it, the display you use is likely to make a more noticeable difference.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With GTA 6 bringing players back to Vice City, many are already thinking about how to get the most out of Rockstar’s next open-world game when it rolls out.

With neon-lit streets, crowded nightlife, tropical beaches and surrounding landscapes of Leonida, GTA 6 is Rockstar’s most visually ambitious release yet.

While much of the conversation is focused on how consoles will handle it, the display you use is likely to make a more noticeable difference.

OLED technology has become increasingly popular thanks to its deep blacks, strong contrast, and vibrant colors. For a game featuring the diverse environments shown in GTA 6’s trailers, and especially paired with HDR, those advantages make upgrading your display the obvious choice.

Sources indicate that unlike traditional LCD monitors, OLED displays can turn individual pixels off completely, producing those luxuriously deep blacks. That will make GTA 6’s neon-lit streets, nighttime environments, and colorful landscapes look far more impressive.

For GTA 6, those improvements will be particularly noticeable in several environments players have already seen in Rockstar’s trailers:.

Modern OLED gaming monitors have also introduced technologies designed to improve brightness and visibility across different environments.

It has been revealed that GIGABYTE’s AORUS FO32U24G features a 32-inch 4K display built around a fourth-generation Tandem WOLED panel. Its RealBlack Glossy screen treatment is designed to preserve deep blacks and perceived contrast while reducing reflections.

It has been revealed that the monitor also features HyperNits, a technology that adjusts HDR brightness to help prevent images from appearing overly dark. According to GIGABYTE, HyperNits can increase overall brightness by up to 30% while preserving highlight details.

That will be particularly relevant to GTA 6’s varied environments, where players will frequently transition between bright sunlight, darker interiors, and nighttime scenes.

Although high-end gaming monitors are often associated with PC gaming, OLED’s picture quality advantages aren’t limited to players with expensive gaming computers.

GTA 6 is scheduled to launch on PS5, PS5 Pro, and Xbox Series X|S.

Both the PS5 and Xbox Series X|S support modern display features, including HDR and up to 120Hz output in compatible games.

For console players, there are three main display features worth considering:.

GIGABYTE’s FO32U24G and FO27Q28G both feature HDMI 2.1 connectivity, making them options for players who use their monitors with consoles as well as PCs.

And while consoles won’t maximise these monitors’ refresh rates of 240Hz and 280Hz, OLED’s visual improvements will be just as glorious.

Even at lower frame rates, OLED’s contrast, black levels, and color reproduction will improve how supported games look. Of course, GTA 6’s final rendering resolution and performance modes remain dependent on Rockstar’s implementation.

Despite the advantages of OLED, burn-in remains one of the most common concerns surrounding the technology.

Burn-in occurs when uneven pixel wear leaves persistent image retention on a display. This can become a consideration when static elements remain visible for extended periods, including health bars, mini-maps, and other interface elements commonly found in video games.

For a game like GTA 6, where players could spend hundreds of hours exploring the open world, long-term display protection is worth considering.

GIGABYTE addresses this with AI OLED Care Pro, available on the AORUS FO32U24G and FO27Q28G. The system automatically manages brightness, performs pixel cleaning during idle periods, and powers down the display when users step away.

It also includes Cooling Force technology, which uses integrated heat pipes to help manage panel temperatures during extended use.

While OLED technology offers several advantages, choosing the right display involves more than simply deciding between OLED and LCD.

Screen size, resolution, panel technology, and room lighting can all influence which monitor makes the most sense.

For players prioritizing GTA 6’s visual presentation, GIGABYTE’s FO32U24G offers a 32-inch 4K Tandem WOLED panel, while the FO27Q28G provides a smaller 27-inch QHD alternative with a 280Hz refresh rate.

GIGABYTE’s M series also includes several options for players with different preferences:.

In a recent development, the MO27Q28G and MO27Q28GR are particularly relevant for players deciding between matte-style anti-reflection and glossy OLED displays. Both feature fourth-generation Tandem WOLED panels, but their different screen treatments may appeal to different gaming environments.

Meanwhile, the MO27Q2A provides an alternative OLED panel technology, featuring QD-OLED panel with 1.5M:1 contrast ratio for deeper black and richer details.

Ultimately, choosing a monitor for GTA 6 depends on the display someone already owns and what they want to improve, but OLED’s contrast, black levels, and color reproduction will provide a noticeable visual upgrade.

Every developer has shipped the other kind of page: a lovingly written article or landing page that peaks on launch day and then quietly rots. Screenshots age, statistics expire, rankings slide. Data-driven pages play the opposite game. Built from a living dataset, they republish themselves daily, grow to thousands of URLs, and answer questions nobody had asked when the site launched. This guide breaks down how they work, using a real fan-run stats site as the running example: one public dataset in, more than ten thousand fresh pages out.

Industry observers note that static pages lose ground because the web moves and they do not. Facts expire, competitors publish fresher answers, and search engines reward pages whose information matches today. A page that cannot enhancement itself must be rewritten by hand, so most sites update a few pages and abandon the rest.

Freshness is not one rule for the whole web; it depends on the query. Nobody needs a CSS tutorial rewritten weekly, but statistics, prices, availability and anything with a season attached decays on a schedule. Developers misjudge this constantly, treating every page like documentation when half their catalogue is really a perishable good. Serve a three-month-old stat as if it were current and readers learn the most damaging lesson a site can teach: do not trust the numbers here.

Then there is the maintenance maths. A hundred hand-written pages each needing one review a year is a hundred small debts, and the interest compounds as the catalogue grows. The team updates the flagship pages, promises to return for the rest, and quietly never does. Data-driven architecture is really a staffing decision disguised as a technical one: humans design the system once, and the system does the updating forever.

A data-driven site has three layers: a dataset that refreshes on a schedule, templates that turn records into pages, and URL patterns that map every meaningful combination users might search for. Change the data and every page changes; improve a template and ten thousand pages improve at once.

The running example makes this concrete. A fan-built Overwatch stats tracker republishes Blizzard's public hero data on a daily cycle. From that one feed it generates hero profiles, head-to-head matchup pages and multi-condition tier lists: 10,291 URLs in its sitemap, across six languages, with matchup pages alone accounting for 8,586 of them. Nobody wrote those pages. Somebody designed the system that writes them, which is a very different, and much more scalable, job.

The example runs on Next.js behind a CDN, but the stack is the least key layer of the three. The same pipeline feeding WordPress, Astro or a static site generator would look identical from the reader's side of the glass. Choose boring technology you already know, and spend your originality budget on the dataset and the templates, because that is where readers will feel the difference.

Generated pages stay useful when every URL must earn its existence with data. Set minimum thresholds before a page is published, give each template unique modules its siblings do not have, and noindex combinations with nothing to say. The line between a resource and spam is not automation; it is emptiness.

Quality gates work best when they are public and mechanical. The example site publishes its tier formula openly: 70% of the score from win rate, 30% from pick rate, and a hard floor that excludes heroes picked in under 0.5% of matches from topping the ranking, because a tiny sample cannot prove anything. That single floor is editorial policy expressed as code. Your version might be a minimum number of data points, a minimum price history, or a minimum review count — the number matters less than the fact that the gate exists and applies to every page equally.

According to recent reports, each template also needs modules its siblings cannot copy. A hero profile carries a seven-day trend and its best and worst matchups; a matchup page carries the head-to-head history; a tier list carries the movement since yesterday. Add a short human layer on top — a methodology page explaining the scoring, changelogs narrating what moved — and the catalogue stops reading as output and starts reading as a publication. Google's scaled-content rules target pages manufactured to manipulate rankings with little value; a page that answers a real query with real, current data is the opposite of that. The honest test for any generated URL is simple: if it vanished tonight, would a searcher lose an answer?

Start embarrassingly small: one dataset, one entity type, one template. A football club's results archive, a property portal's sold prices, your own product catalogue — anything structured and refreshed beats a grand plan. Prove one template earns traffic, then add combinations, languages and dashboards in that order.

What is programmatic SEO? Programmatic SEO means generating many pages from a structured dataset using templates, instead of writing each page by hand. Done well, each page answers a distinct search with real data. Done badly, it produces thousands of near-identical pages, which is where its reputation suffers.

Industry observers note that is programmatic SEO against Google's rules? No. Google's spam policies target scaled content created mainly to manipulate rankings, with little or no value for consumers. Pages generated from real data that answer real queries are publishing. The deciding question is whether a page helps its reader, not how it was produced.

Sources indicate that how often should the data behind pages refresh? Match the refresh to how fast the underlying facts change. Sports and game statistics justify daily pulls, prices often need hourly checks, and reference data may only move monthly. Refreshing faster than reality changes wastes crawl budget and makes 'updated' stamps meaningless.

Sources indicate that do generated pages need unique written text? They need unique value, which is not the same thing. Identical paragraphs on ten thousand pages add nothing, but unique data, comparisons and trends are content in their own right. Add short human-written context per template, and let the data carry the differences between pages.

How many pages should a first project launch with? Launch with the smallest set that proves the template: one entity type, a few hundred pages at most. Validate that search engines index them and users engage before adding combinations and languages. Scaling an unproven template just manufactures tomorrow's cleanup job at industrial size.

It has been revealed that the sites quietly winning the long game are not publishing more; they are publishing systems. One honest dataset, one well-built template and strict quality gates will outlast a hundred hand-written pages competing on freshness alone. Try it this week: take one dataset you already own, design a single template with four real modules, and ship fifty pages. Watch what the data does next.
